props.title: The Business
props.initialSlug: Young Brit rises in Spain's brutal drug trade '80s

sections.content: The Business represents a gritty peak in British gangster cinema, following the path carved by earlier hits like Layer Cake (2004) and Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels (1998). Danny Dyer delivers one of his most compelling performances as Frankie, a South London criminal who escapes to Spain's Costa del Sol - nicknamed the Costa del Crime due to the real influx of British gangsters in the 1980s. The film captures the sun-drenched excess of the era, complete with period-perfect fashion, music, and a cocaine-fueled nightclub scene that defined the decade.

sections.content: The film sits within a broader tradition of British crime cinema exploring expatriate criminals, like The Long Good Friday (1980) and Sexy Beast (2000). Director Nick Love brings his signature raw energy while painting a vivid picture of the 1980s Spanish underworld. The film's attention to period detail - from the flashy Mercedes cars to the pastel-heavy wardrobe - creates an authentic snapshot of an era when British criminals viewed Spain as their personal playground. SUBHEAD: Crime in the Sun: The Costa del Crime Legacy

The Business taps into the real phenomenon of British criminals fleeing to Spain to avoid prosecution, thanks to the lack of extradition treaties at the time. This same criminal exodus inspired films like Essex Boys (2000) and elements of Sexy Beast (2000), creating a distinct sub-genre of British crime films set in the Spanish sunshine. The contrast between violent criminality and Mediterranean luxury became a powerful motif in these films, reflecting the real tension between escapist fantasy and brutal reality.
